Series::isposinf¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::isposinf() const

Identify Only Positive Infinity¶

isposinf() performs an elementwise directional infinity test. It returns true exactly where the receiver contains positive infinity. Finite positive values, either signed zero, negative infinity, and NaN return false.

The method is intended for logic where positive overflow or an unbounded upper result must be distinguished from negative overflow. If direction does not matter, isinf() states that intent directly. If all invalid floating values matter, combine the relevant infinity mask with isnan().

The result is a newly allocated Boolean Series. Rank, shape, lane order, and platform are preserved; dtype is always bool. Integral and Boolean receivers are valid and yield all false because those dtypes have no infinity encoding. Complex receivers are rejected because positive and negative ordering is not defined for a complex value. Project real() or imag() first when a specific component is what should be classified.

Predicate output is non-differentiable. It intentionally forms no reverse-mode node, regardless of whether the receiver tracks sensitivity.

Examples¶

Example 1. Only positive infinity matches; positive finite values and NaN do not.

const double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
const double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
auto x = pluss::make_series({-inf, -1.0, -0.0, 0.0, 1.0, inf, nan});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.isposinf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[false, false, false, false, false, true, false]

Example 2. Matrix structure survives unchanged while each lane is classified.

const double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
const double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
auto x = pluss::make_series({{-inf, 2.0}, {inf, nan}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.isposinf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ false false ⎤
⎣  true false ⎦

Example 3. An integer receiver produces a shape-preserving all-false mask.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2, 0, 2}).isposinf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[false, false, false]

Example 4. Directional masks can be used independently before being joined. The joined mask still excludes NaN.

const double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
const double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
auto x = pluss::make_series({-inf, -1.0, -0.0, 0.0, 1.0, inf, nan});
pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    x.isneginf().logical_or(x.isposinf()));

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false, false, false, false, true, false]

Example 5. Complex input is rejected rather than assigned an arbitrary order.

try {
  using Complex = std::complex<double>;
  const double inf = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
  (void)pluss::make_series(std::vector<Complex>{{inf, 0.0}}, {1})
      .isposinf();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  const std::string message = e.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

isposinf: complex input is not supported

See Also¶

  • isneginf() selects negative infinity only.

  • isinf() selects infinity in either direction.

  • isfinite() selects finite values.

  • isnan() selects not-a-number values.
